name: Idi Amin

meta.summary: Idi Amin seized power in a January 1971 military coup, dissolved parliament, suspended parts of the constitution, banned political parties, and ruled by decree, declaring himself President for Life in 1976. His regime's security organs (the State Research Bureau, Public Safety Unit, and Military Police) carried out mass detention, torture, and extrajudicial killings, with death-toll estimates ranging from roughly 80,000 to 500,000; high-profile victims included Chief Justice Benedicto Kiwanuka and Archbishop Janani Luwum. In 1972 he expelled around 80,000 Ugandan Asians, and his rule ended in 1979 after a failed invasion of Tanzania triggered a counter-invasion that captured Kampala.

editor_note: Our incompetence anchor: competence rated very low (15) despite near-total capture of every domain (all six condition indicators fire). Death-toll-dependent claims flagged medium; specific well-documented single acts (Luwum killing, President-for-Life, Asian expulsion) high.

scored_actions.note: After the coup Amin placed military tribunals above the civil courts and had the sitting Chief Justice murdered, leaving no independent judicial review of executive acts.
Amin's government defied Chief Justice Kiwanuka's writ of habeas corpus ordering the release of a detained businessman from military detention.
Chief Justice Benedicto Kiwanuka was abducted at gunpoint from his High Court chambers and killed the next day, removing the country's top independent judge.
Amin placed military tribunals above the system of civil law, routing cases (including for civilians) to loyal military courts.
Amin seized power by coup in 1971 and held no national election of any kind during the entire eight-year regime.

sources.title: Idi Amin Overthrows President Milton Obote in Uganda

scored_actions.note: Despite promising a return to civilian rule and elections after the coup, Amin held none and indefinitely suspended the electoral provisions of the constitution.
The Defense Council declared Amin President for Life, permanently extending his tenure with no limit.
Amin banned all political parties, dissolving the multi-party framework and outlawing the opposition entirely.
Newspapers were nationalised or banned and the press reduced to a handful of regime-friendly outlets, leaving no independent mass media.

scored_actions.note: The influential Luganda Catholic newspaper Munno was banned in 1976, part of Amin's nationalisation/closure of independent papers.
Journalists were routinely detained and jailed for their work as censorship and closures gripped the industry.

scored_actions.note: The regime imposed pervasive censorship on the press throughout the decade.
Movement and assembly were tightly controlled through security decrees and a climate of fear documented by Amnesty International.
The State Research Bureau, Public Safety Unit, and Military Police detained civilians en masse without trial; toll estimates (contested) run from ~80,000 to 500,000 dead.

sources.title: Uganda: Idi Amin Dies Without Facing Justice

scored_actions.note: With parliament dissolved, the judiciary decapitated, and rule by decree, no institution could constrain the executive.
Amin dissolved parliament and vested all legislative powers of the constitution in himself.
Amin governed by presidential decree, issuing roughly 30 decrees in place of legislation.
The regime routinely imprisoned, tortured, and killed perceived opponents through its security organs.

sources.title: Uganda: Idi Amin Dies Without Facing Justice

scored_actions.note: Systematic massacres targeted Acholi and Langi soldiers and civilians (Obote's ethnic base) in the regime's first years.

sources.title: Uganda: Idi Amin Dies Without Facing Justice

scored_actions.note: Widespread extrajudicial killings and disappearances, including Archbishop Janani Luwum, shot dead and falsely reported killed in a car crash.
Cabinet ministers Erinayo Oryema and Charles Oboth-Ofumbi were arrested with Luwum and killed; earlier, DP leader/CJ Kiwanuka was detained and murdered.
The State Research Bureau ran notorious torture facilities (Nakasero, Kampala) where detainees were systematically brutalised.
Amin ordered the expulsion of roughly 80,000 Ugandan Asians within 90 days and cancelled outstanding citizenship applications (~12,000), forcing many into statelessness and exile.

sources.title: Ugandan Asians: 50 years since their expulsion

harm.basis: Estimated 80,000-500,000 killed (widely contested) by the security organs, plus ~80,000 Asians expelled -- a very high toll relative to Uganda's ~11 million population.

wins: The January 1971 coup was well-timed and near-bloodless: Amin took Kampala and the army while President Obote was abroad.
Built a loyalty-based terror state (State Research Bureau, Public Safety Unit) from his own base, which kept him in power for nearly eight years.
Short-term populism and patronage: the 1972 'economic war' and Africanisation of Asian-owned businesses bought early army and popular support.
failures: The 1972 expulsion of ~80,000 Asians handed businesses to unqualified cronies and collapsed trade, commerce, and tax revenue.
Purged the army along ethnic lines, murdering experienced Acholi and Langi officers and hollowing out the military.
Invaded Tanzania's Kagera Salient in late 1978, provoking a counter-invasion that captured Kampala and toppled him in April 1979.
Alienated nearly every foreign backer through mercurial diplomacy, leaving Uganda isolated when the regime collapsed.
